summary: This informational memo documents MAPOS, a multiple access protocol that carries network datagrams, wrapped in HDLC frames, over SONET/SDH links.

eli5.summary: Rules for many devices to share a fast fiber line and take turns sending.

subtitle: How HDLC frames are sent over SONET/SDH so that many nodes can share a switched fiber network.

tldr.problem: SONET/SDH links are inherently point-to-point, which makes it hard to build a LAN or WAN with several nodes on them.
tldr.mechanism: MAPOS puts HDLC-like frames with an 8-bit destination address into SONET/SDH payloads, and a frame switch forwards each frame to its destination by that address.
tldr.outcome: The result is a connectionless, switched, broadcast and multicast capable link layer that can carry any network protocol such as IP. The memo is Informational and not an IETF standard.

today: RFC 2171 is an Informational memo from June 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The authors note it is not the product of an IETF working group and is not a standards track document.

sections.title: What MAPOS Does
sections.content:
MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) transmits network-protocol datagrams, encapsulated in HDLC frames, over SONET/SDH. SONET/SDH is a family of ITU-T standard protocols for broadband optical fiber transmission, and it is an inherently point-to-point link. MAPOS adds multiple access to it, so SONET/SDH can be used as the medium for both LAN and WAN.

The protocol is connection-less. A node fills in the destination address of an HDLC frame, places it in one or more SONET/SDH payloads and sends it. A switch forwards the frame by its destination address, across several switches if needed. Broadcast and multicast are supported, and frames with an invalid destination address are silently discarded. Because MAPOS is a link layer protocol it is independent of upper layers, and the memo says it can support any network layer protocol such as IP.
sections.eli5: A fiber line normally joins just two ends. MAPOS lets lots of computers share it, a bit like a post office sorting parcels by address.

sections.title: Configurations and Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC shows three configurations: two nodes connected directly (point-to-point), a star of end nodes around one frame switch, and several frame switches linked into a switching cluster. The switch provides the multiple access capability, as in Ethernet.

Each switch port has an identifier that is unique within the switch, and a node connected to a port inherits that port's address. In a cluster, the address is subnetted: the high-order bits, where the subnet mask has 1s, give the switch address and the low-order bits give the node within the switch. The address can be set manually or by the address assignment mechanism in RFC 2173. Any two components may be joined directly or over a long-haul SONET/SDH leased line.
sections.eli5: Each plug on the switch has a number, and whatever is plugged in uses that number as its address. In a big network the address says both which switch and which plug.

sections.title: The HDLC Frame Format
sections.content:
MAPOS uses the same HDLC-like framing as PPP over SONET, described in RFC 1662. LLC and SNAP are not used. A frame has a Flag, Address, Control, Protocol, Information, FCS and a closing Flag.

  • Flag: 01111110 (0x7E) begins and ends each frame, and is sent continuously when the line is idle.
  • Address: 8 bits holding the destination. The least significant bit is always 1. The top bit is 0 for unicast and 1 for multicast, with six bits of node or group address between. 0xFF means broadcast, and 0x01 is reserved for the control processor inside a switch.
  • Control: always 00000011 (0x03), Unnumbered Information. Frames with any other value are silently discarded.
  • Protocol: 16 bits naming the protocol of the payload, with values from the Assigned Numbers documents.
  • Information: the datagram, at most 65,280 octets (64K - 256).
  • FCS: 16 bits by default, optionally 32 bits.
sections.eli5: Every parcel has start and end markers, a delivery address, a note saying what is inside, and a check number to spot damage.

sections.title: Octet-Synchronous Framing
sections.content:
MAPOS treats SONET/SDH as a byte-oriented synchronous link, so it uses octet stuffing. Because SONET/SDH provides transparency, the Async-Control-Character-Map (ACCM) is not used. Frames are separated by one or more flag sequences.

After the FCS is computed and before sending, each 0x7E inside a frame becomes 0x7D 0x5E, and each 0x7D becomes 0x7D 0x5D. The receiver reverses this before computing the FCS. The sender must also fill gaps between frames with flag sequences, and must abort and keep sending flags if a DMA under-run occurs.
sections.eli5: The start marker is a special pattern, so if that pattern shows up inside a parcel it is swapped for a code the receiver knows how to turn back.

sections.title: SONET and SDH Differences
sections.content:
The physical layer is treated as a transparent channel that delivers HDLC frames unaltered. Nodes and switches should terminate section, line and path overhead, but SONET and SDH interpret overhead differently and some implementations use overhead bytes in proprietary ways. Appendix A lists the main trouble spots and urges implementors to provide workaround options.

Examples are the SS bits in the H1 byte of the AU pointer (set differently by SONET and SDH for OC-3c), the reserved Z1 and Z2 bytes, and the D bytes of the Data Communication channel. The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.eli5: Two fiber systems can read the same label slightly differently, so builders should be ready to adjust settings when parts do not agree.

items.title: Unicast
items.text: Top bit 0, six bits of node address, last bit 1.

items.title: Multicast
items.text: Top bit 1, six bits of group address, last bit 1.

items.title: Switch control
items.text: The address 0x01 is reserved for the control processor inside a switch.
